title: AI Debt Is Crowding Out Treasuries, and the US Economy Is Actually in Deflation
dek: AI capex has grown big enough to push into the Treasury market and distort global trade and inflation data; strip out the AI-related parts and the US economy is mildly deflationary, while the Fed is hiking for the wrong reasons.
why: Paul Kedrosky strings how AI capex seeps into Treasuries, trade and inflation into a single causal chain, and the back half on an Anthropic IPO and OpenAI's valuation is especially dense.
who: Investors and founders watching the intersection of macro and AI capex, and engineers who want to know which specific link in the chain cracks first when the AI bubble bursts.
skip: The small talk from 0:06 to 1:06 at the start can be skipped.

points.h: AI capex can now move Treasury yields
points.body: Over the past 12 to 18 months, AI capex has consistently accounted for 30% to 70% of US GDP growth. More anomalous is that it has started to seep into the Treasury market: AI-related debt issuance is approaching $1 trillion, and debt's share of AI financing has risen from 15% to 20% a year ago to over 60%, making it the single largest block in both the investment-grade and high-yield markets. The result is that yield-sensitive investors would rather hold hyperscaler debt than Treasuries at the same duration, pushing the 10-year yield up. Kedrosky stresses this is not the market losing faith in America's ability to pay — the US can print money and will not default — it is competition at the margin.

points.h: More than half of global trade growth is AI
points.body: The WTO had forecast that global goods trade would fall noticeably because of US tariff policy; instead it grew about 4.5%, close to double the forecast. Digging into the data to find out why, the WTO found that over the past three quarters 19% of global goods trade was AI-related, and close to 55% of global trade growth was AI-related — mostly NVIDIA GPUs. Kedrosky's conclusion: AI capex is masking the real impact of Trump's tariffs, because it is so large it drowns out every other signal.

points.h: Both sources of US inflation point back to AI
points.body: US inflation is still above 3%, yet consumers are more stretched and more indebted than they have been in a long time. Break inflation apart and the two biggest pieces are: first, AI capex pushing up energy prices, which pushes up construction costs, materials and all kinds of services; second, the energy shock from the Iran war. Kedrosky counts the latter as AI-related too — he argues the Trump administration was emboldened by the success of the operation it ran in Venezuela using Anthropic, turned war into an app, and Iran is next. So both preconditions for inflation sit on top of AI.

points.h: Strip out AI and the US is in deflation
points.body: If you remove AI-capex-related inflation and the energy inflation from the AI-emboldened Iran war from the US economy, Kedrosky calculates the US is actually running about 0.25% deflation. That means the Fed is hiking for the wrong reasons — it thinks it is suppressing demand-side inflation, when the actual inflation is exogenous. This resembles the path into the 1929 crash: high rates plus a weak consumer are the classic precursors of a long balance sheet recession. He cites Richard Koo's work on Japan's lost decade and argues all the conditions are now in place.

points.h: Balance sheet recession: a decade of deleveraging, no spending, no hiring
points.body: Hyperscalers will not go bankrupt, but they will spend a decade cleaning up their balance sheets — going from the least indebted companies in the market to the most indebted. A balance sheet recession is when companies focus on deleveraging and getting debt off the books regardless of the level of rates. The consequence: no investment in growth, no hiring, while simultaneously looking for ways to use AI to cut headcount. Companies like CoreWeave face a different problem — rolling over debt over the next five years may force them into some form of insolvency. Kedrosky says this will be the most underrated macro event of the next five years.

points.h: The system is screaming: data center financing costs are rising on their own
points.body: The 10-year yield has risen about 100 basis points over the past few months, directly raising the financing cost of new data centers. But it goes further: when the system is under stress, the spread between issuance yields and the 10-year widens from 100 basis points to 150 or even 200. So every time you see rates rise, you should translate it as "data centers just got a lot harder at proving their future cash flows." Kedrosky judges that from a financing-cost standpoint this breaks within 6 to 12 months — the most stressed end of the market is demanding 11% to 12% returns, which is impossible to deliver.

points.h: Data centers need to earn 7%, but nobody can make the math work
points.body: The investment-grade market currently demands a median return of about 7.2% from data centers, and junk grade demands 10%. But Kedrosky stresses this is the threshold to attract creditors, not the threshold to get your capital back — that is a separate question, and he thinks it simply cannot be earned back. He coined the term EBBT — earnings before bad things — where you cut out all the spending and of course the cash flow looks great, but that assumes hyperscalers stop burning money on frontier models, and nobody is doing that. If you only do industrial-grade inference, then it is fundamentally an energy problem: China adds roughly 3x the new energy capacity the US does each year, and is already ahead.

points.h: Anthropic's IPO slipped from October to November, and employees are borrowing millions to exercise
points.body: What Kedrosky has heard is that Anthropic originally planned to IPO on October 1, and it has now reportedly been pushed to November. His general rule: even in a good market, at least half the companies that say they will list by year-end do not make it that year. Internally there is panic about what an IPO this year would look like. More concretely, employees: many have already exercised their options, and if the IPO does not happen they face the IRS's AMT, generating tax bills in the millions — he knows quite a few people who have borrowed millions of dollars for this. He also mentions a supplier close to the company saying Anthropic's third quarter came in below expectations, but stresses this is rumor, and consistent with the backdrop of customer concentration and token maxing fading.

So if I cut out all of the things that are costing me a lot of money, and then I calculate EBBT, not EBIT, but EBBT, earnings before bad things, then my cash flow is tremendous.

And so we're now in this moment where the companies at the center of all of this are in this kind of Minsky moment where the financialization of what they're doing is so large and so broad it's affecting everything. But at the same time, they're all very eager to dump the shares and get them out there at a credibly large scale to retail investors.
